title: The most ambiguous RNA under base-pair maximization
statement: In the base-pair maximization (Nussinov) model an RNA sequence over A, C, G, U folds into a secondary structure: a set of base pairs from {AU, UA, GC, CG, GU, UG}, each base in at most one pair, every pair (i, j) with j - i >= 4 (a hairpin loop of at least three bases), and no two pairs crossing (i < k < j < l). The predicted structures are those with the largest number of pairs. Let N(s) be the number of such optimal structures of the sequence s and D(n) the largest N(s) over sequences of length n. Determine D(n); the headline cell is n = 30: find a sequence of length 30 with more than 100,603 optimal structures.
submission: Text file: an RNA sequence of length 30 over A, C, G, U (whitespace and lines starting with # are ignored).
score: the number N(s) of structures with the maximum number of base pairs, computed exactly by the checker (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the sequence UUUUUUGGCAUCGGGAAAAAAAAAGGGAGA (7 pairs, 100,603 optimal structures), found by simulated annealing over sequences (tools/src/nussdeg.c)

context: Base-pair maximization (Nussinov and Jacobson, PNAS 1980) is the simplest RNA folding model and the core of the dynamic programs behind energy-based prediction; its optimum is often far from unique, and the number of co-optimal and suboptimal structures is how prediction ambiguity is measured (Wuchty, Fontana, Hofacker and Schuster, Biopolymers 1999). The total number of secondary structures of a length-n chain grows exponentially (Stein and Waterman 1979); D(n) asks how much of that can be concentrated on the optimum by one sequence, a worst case for structure prediction. The exact first values below grow quickly (D(13) = 63) and the best sequences found mix G-U wobble stretches with A-U and G-C blocks, but neither the growth rate of D(n) nor the shape of the extremal sequences is known.
references: R. Nussinov, A. B. Jacobson, Fast algorithm for predicting the secondary structure of single-stranded RNA, PNAS 77 (1980) 6309-6313
P. R. Stein, M. S. Waterman, On some new sequences generalizing the Catalan and Motzkin numbers, Discrete Math. 26 (1979) 261-272
S. Wuchty, W. Fontana, I. L. Hofacker, P. Schuster, Complete suboptimal folding of RNA and the stability of secondary structures, Biopolymers 49 (1999) 145-165

novelty.verdict: new. No paper, table or OEIS entry was found for the largest number of co-optimal structures under base-pair maximization; the exact sequence D(1), ..., D(13) is not in the OEIS.
closest: Counting of all secondary structures (Stein-Waterman numbers) and suboptimal-structure enumeration for given sequences; neither maximizes the number of optimal structures over sequences.

first_values.note: Exact values: every sequence of length n (tools/src/nussdeg.c exhaustive). Best known values: simulated annealing over sequences, 60 s each. Trivial upper bound: the number of all secondary structures on n bases (568 for n = 13, 240,944,076 for n = 30).

baseline.text: 100,603 for n = 30, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the sequence in `refs/nussinov-degeneracy.txt`. Upper bound 240,944,076, the number of all secondary structures of a 30-base chain with hairpins of at least 3 bases.

bound.source: all secondary structures on 30 bases with hairpin loops of at least 3
